sources.title: Self-Care Monitoring of Heart Failure Symptoms and Lung Impedance at Home Following Hospital Discharge: Longitudinal Study

evidence.claim: The prospective longitudinal study included 10 participants with NYHA class III or IV heart failure and used caregiver-assisted measurements.
evidence.study_context: Two university hospitals in Norway and Lithuania; severe heart failure; informal caregivers aided measurements.

evidence.claim: Seven participants provided data for the full 30-day assessment period.
evidence.limitations: Three participants did not provide the full planned period.

evidence.claim: The study received 262 of 300 planned impedance measurements, or 87 percent.
evidence.limitations: Measurements were caregiver-assisted and technical support was available.

evidence.claim: The study received 1332 of 1500 planned symptom-diary entries, or 89 percent.
evidence.study_context: Daily symptom diary during the 30-day assessment.
evidence.limitations: Completion was observed in a small supported pilot.

evidence.claim: All participants had daily contact with the heart-failure study nurse, a level of access not included in routine follow-up in the two countries.
evidence.study_context: SMS or phone contact and technical feedback were available.
evidence.limitations: The support condition limits transfer to routine care.

evidence.claim: The median standardized self-care score increased from 56 to 81 over 30 days, with P=.007.
evidence.limitations: The longitudinal design does not isolate the effect of the monitoring tools.

evidence.claim: The small sample and variability precluded analysis of symptom-impedance associations, and the daily symptom instrument was not validated for this use.
evidence.limitations: Predictive and association claims are not supported.

evidence.claim: A larger future study was needed to determine predictive utility; reduced readmissions were presented as a possibility rather than an established effect.
evidence.study_context: Future-research statement in the full text.
evidence.limitations: Do not report prediction or readmission reduction as a study result.

claims.text: The study was a small prospective longitudinal pilot of 10 participants with caregiver-assisted measurements.
The observed completion rates support 30-day process feasibility under the study support conditions.
claims.boundary: Applies to the 10-participant pilot with caregiver assistance and daily nurse access, not routine-care effectiveness.

claims.text: The median self-care score increased from 56 to 81 during the 30-day follow-up, with P=.007.
The monitoring tools caused the increase in self-care score.
claims.boundary: No control group separated monitoring from time, caregiver assistance, or nurse contact.

claims.text: The study did not establish predictive utility or reduced readmissions.
